title: Spontaneous Uses of Typicality in Narratives of Positive and Negative Inter‐Ethnic Contact in a Scottish Community
abstract: ABSTRACT Research on intergroup contact shows that positive encounters are more likely to improve attitudes when the outgroup member involved is viewed as typical of their group. However, existing studies have treated typicality as a researcher‐defined cognitive judgement, leaving unclear whether and how people spontaneously invoke typicality when making sense of everyday contact experiences. We addressed this question through 25 semi‐structured interviews with adults of migrant and non‐migrant backgrounds living in an ethnically diverse area of North‐East Scotland. Using a qualitative narrative analysis, we examined how participants interpreted contact events and situated them within a broader narrative of intergroup relations. Participants deployed various strategies to frame contact events as typical or atypical of the group concerned. These included appeals to frequency, exceptionality, subgroup membership and emphasising personal characteristics. Framing contact as atypical enabled some participants to acknowledge experiences that contradicted their overall stance towards an outgroup, while framing contact as typical supported generalisation. Typicality therefore functioned as a narrative resource which may enable reconciliation of multiple and sometimes conflicting contact experiences within a coherent narrative of self and other. We argue that generalisation of contact events is shaped not only by cognitive categorisation processes but also by narrative processes of meaning‐making.
